[Peter T. Tanksley]{.masthead-name}

[]{.belt-bar}

[Research Scientist, ALERRT Center · Texas State University]{.masthead-role}

::: {.masthead-thesis}
I study the people who run toward emergencies, and what all that running does to them. Most of my work asks how being a first responder shapes health and mortality, using national death-certificate data and the occasional vial of blood. The rest is about police: how they're trained to make hard calls in seconds, and why the public and the officers watching the same call so rarely agree on it.
:::

<h2 class="section-head">What I work on</h2>

::: {.pillars}
::: {.pillar}
### First responder health and mortality
How officers and firefighters die, and which parts of the job get them there. The evidence is death certificates from across the country, blood drawn in fire stations, and the workers' compensation laws that decide whether any of it counts as work-related.

[Read more →](research.qmd#health){.more}
:::

::: {.pillar}
### Police training and public opinion
How officers are trained to make the worst decision of their week in under two seconds, and how that decision looks afterward to the public versus the people who make them. Spoiler: the two audiences did not watch the same encounter.

[Read more →](research.qmd#training){.more}
:::
:::
:::
::::
